If our youngest brother is with us, then we will go down: for we may not see the man⌘’s face, unless our youngest brother is with us.’✦ 27 Your servant, my father, said to us, ‘You know that my wife bore me two sons.✦ 28 One went out from me, and I said, “Surely he is torn in pieces;” and I haven’t seen him since.✦ 29 If you take this one also from me, and harm happens to him, you will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to Sheol.’✦ 30 Now therefore when I come to your servant my father, and the boy is not with us; since his life is bound up in the boy’s life;✦ 31 it will happen, when he sees that the boy is no more, that he will die. Your servants will bring down the gray hairs of your servant, our father, with sorrow to Sheol.✦ 32 For your servant became collateral for the boy to my father, saying, ‘If I don’t bring him to you, then I will bear the blame to my father forever.’✦ 33 Now therefore, please let your servant stay instead of the boy◇, my lord⌘’s slave; and let the boy go up with his brothers.✦ 34 For how will I go up to my father, if the boy isn’t with me?—lest I see the evil that will come on my father.”

45

✦1 Then Joseph couldn’t control himself before all those who stood before him, and he called out, “Cause everyone to go out from me!” No one else stood with him, while Joseph made himself known to his brothers.⌘✦ 2 He wept aloud. The Egyptians heard, and the house of Pharaoh heard.✦ 3 Joseph said to his brothers, “I am Joseph! Does my father still live?” His brothers couldn’t answer him; for they were terrified at his presence.✦ 4 Joseph said to his brothers, “Come near to me, please.” They came near. He said, “I am Joseph, your brother◇, whom you sold into Egypt.◇✦ 5 Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God⌘ sent me before you to preserve life◇.‖✦◇ 6 For these two years the famine has been in the land⌘, and there are yet five years, in which there will be no plowing and no harvest.✦⌂⌂ 7 God⌘ sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant◇ in the earth⌘, and to save you alive by a great deliverance.✦ 8 So now it wasn’t you who sent me here, but God⌘◇, and he has made me a father to Pharaoh, lord⌘ of all his house, and ruler over all the land⌘ of Egypt.✦ 9 Hurry, and go up to my father, and tell him, ‘This is what your son Joseph says, “God⌘ has made me lord⌘ of all Egypt. Come down to me. Don’t wait.✦ 10 You shall dwell in the land⌘ of Goshen, and you will be near to me, you, your children, your children’s children, your flocks, your herds, and all that you have.✦⌂ 11 There I will provide for you; for there are yet five years of famine; lest you come to poverty, you, and your household, and all that you have.”’✦ 12 Behold, your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin, that it is my mouth that speaks to you.✦ 13 You shall tell my father of all my glory⌘ in Egypt, and of all that you have seen. You shall hurry and bring my father down here.”✦ 14 He fell on his brother Benjamin’s neck and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck.✦ 15 He kissed all his brothers, and wept on them. After that his brothers talked with him.✦ 16 The report of it was heard in Pharaoh’s house, saying, “Joseph’s brothers have come.” It pleased Pharaoh well, and his servants.✦ 17 Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Tell your brothers, ‘Do this: Load your animals, and go, travel to the land⌘ of Canaan.✦⌂ 18 Take your father and your households, and come to me, and I will give you the good⌘ of the land⌘ of Egypt, and you will eat the fat of the land.’✦ 19 Now you are commanded to do this: Take wagons out of the land⌘ of Egypt for your little ones, and for your wives, and bring your father, and come.✦⌂ 20 Also, don’t concern yourselves about your belongings, for the good⌘ of all the land⌘ of Egypt is yours.”✦ 21 The sons of Israel did so. Joseph gave them wagons, according to the commandment of Pharaoh, and gave them provision for the way. 22 He gave each one of them changes of clothing, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver and five changes of clothing◇.⌘✦⌂ 23 He sent the following to his father: ten donkeys loaded with the good⌘ things of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain and bread and provision for his father by the way. 24 So he sent his brothers away, and they departed. He said to them, “See that you don’t quarrel on the way.”✦ 25 They went up out of Egypt, and came into the land⌘ of Canaan, to Jacob their father. 26 They told him, saying, “Joseph is still alive, and he is ruler over all the land⌘ of Egypt.” His heart⌘ fainted◇, for he didn’t believe them.✦ 27 They told him all the words of Joseph, which he had said to them. When he saw the wagons which Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit⌘ of Jacob, their father, revived.✦ 28 Israel said, “It is enough. Joseph my son is still alive. I will go and see him before I die◇.”

46

✦1 Israel traveled with all that he had, and came to Beersheba, and offered sacrifices to the God⌘ of his father, Isaac.✦ 2 God⌘ spoke to Israel in the visions of the night◇, and said, “Jacob, Jacob!” He said, “Here I am.”✦ 3 He said, “I am God⌘, the God of your father. Don’t be afraid to go down into Egypt◇, for there I will make of you a great nation.⌘✦ 4 I will go down with you into Egypt. I will also surely bring you up again◇. Joseph’s hand will close your eyes.”✦ 5 Jacob rose up from Beersheba, and the sons of Israel carried Jacob, their father, their little ones, and their wives, in the wagons which Pharaoh had sent to carry him.✦ 6 They took their livestock, and their goods, which they had gotten in the land⌘ of Canaan, and came into Egypt—Jacob, and all his offspring with him,✦ 7 his sons, and his sons’ sons with him, his daughters, and his sons’ daughters, and he brought all his offspring with him into Egypt.✦ 8 These are the names of the children of Israel◇, who came into Egypt, Jacob and his sons: Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn.✦ 9 The sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.✦⌂⌂⌂ 10 The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul the son of a Canaanite woman⌘.✦⌂⌂ 11 The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.✦⌂⌂⌂ 12 The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah; but Er and Onan died in the land⌘ of Canaan. The sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul.✦⌂ 13✦⌂⌂ 14 The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Iob, and Shimron. The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.✦⌂ 15 These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan Aram, with his daughter Dinah. All the souls of his sons and his daughters were thirty-three.✦ 16 The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.✦⌂ 17 The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, and Serah their sister. The sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel.✦⌂⌂⌂ 18 These are the sons of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to Leah, his daughter, and these she bore to Jacob, even sixteen souls.✦ 19 The sons of Rachel, Jacob’s wife: Joseph and Benjamin.✦ 20 To Joseph in the land⌘ of Egypt were born Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, bore to him.✦ 21 The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.✦⌂ 22 These are the sons of Rachel, who were born to Jacob: all the souls were fourteen.✦ 23 The son of Dan: Hushim.✦ 24 The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.✦⌂ 25 These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to Rachel, his daughter, and these she bore to Jacob: all the souls were seven.✦ 26 All the souls who came with Jacob into Egypt, who were his direct offspring, in addition to Jacob’s sons’ wives, all the souls were sixty-six.✦ 27 The sons of Joseph, who were born to him in Egypt, were two souls. All the souls of the house of Jacob◇, who came into Egypt, were seventy.✦ 28 Jacob sent Judah before him to Joseph, to show the way before him to Goshen, and they came into the land⌘ of Goshen.✧✦ 29 Joseph prepared his chariot, and went up to meet Israel, his father, in Goshen. He presented himself to him, and fell on his neck, and wept on his neck a good⌘ while◇.✦ 30 Israel said to Joseph, “Now let me die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive.”✦ 31 Joseph said to his brothers, and to his father’s house, “I will go up, and speak with Pharaoh, and will tell him, ‘My brothers, and my father’s house, who were in the land⌘ of Canaan, have come to me.✦ 32 These men are shepherds, for they have been keepers of livestock, and they have brought their flocks, and their herds, and all that they have.’✦ 33 It will happen, when Pharaoh summons you, and will say, ‘What is your occupation?’✦ 34 that you shall say, ‘Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth even until now, both we, and our fathers:’ that you may dwell in the land⌘ of Goshen; for every shepherd is an abomination◇ to the Egyptians.”

47

✦1 Then Joseph went in and told Pharaoh, and said, “My father and my brothers, with their flocks, their herds, and all that they own, have come out of the land⌘ of Canaan; and behold, they are in the land of Goshen.”✧✦ 2 From among his brothers he took five men, and presented them to Pharaoh.✦ 3 Pharaoh said to his brothers, “What is your occupation?” They said to Pharaoh, “Your servants are shepherds, both we, and our fathers.”✦⌂ 4 They also said to Pharaoh, “We have come to live as foreigners in the land⌘, for there is no pasture for your servants’ flocks. For the famine is severe in the land of Canaan. Now therefore, please let your servants dwell in the land of Goshen.”✦ 5 Pharaoh spoke to Joseph, saying, “Your father and your brothers have come to you.✦ 6 The land⌘ of Egypt is before you. Make your father and your brothers dwell in the best of the land. Let them dwell in the land of Goshen◇. If you know any able men among them, then put them in charge of my livestock.”✦⌂ 7 Joseph brought in Jacob, his father, and set him before Pharaoh; and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.✦ 8 Pharaoh said to Jacob, “How old are you?”✦ 9 Jacob said to Pharaoh, “The years of my pilgrimage are one hundred thirty years◇. The days of the years of my life have been few and evil. They have not attained to the days of the years of the life of my fathers in the days of their pilgrimage.”✦ 10 Jacob blessed Pharaoh, and went out from the presence of Pharaoh.✦ 11 Joseph placed his father and his brothers, and gave them a possession in the land⌘ of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded.✦⌂ 12 Joseph provided his father, his brothers, and all of his father’s household with bread, according to the sizes of their families.✦ 13 There was no bread in all the land⌘; for the famine was very severe, so that the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan fainted by reason of the famine.✦ 14 Joseph gathered up all the money◇ that was found in the land⌘ of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, for the grain which they bought: and Joseph brought the money into Pharaoh’s house.✦ 15 When the money was all spent in the land⌘ of Egypt, and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph, and said, “Give us bread, for why should we die in your presence? For our money fails.”✦ 16 Joseph said, “Give me your livestock; and I will give you food for your livestock, if your money is gone.”✦ 17 They brought their livestock to Joseph, and Joseph gave them bread in exchange for the horses, and for the flocks, and for the herds, and for the donkeys: and he fed them with bread in exchange for all their livestock for that year.✦ 18 When that year was ended, they came to him the second year, and said to him, “We will not hide from my lord⌘ how our money is all spent, and the herds of livestock are my lord’s. There is nothing left in the sight of my lord, but our bodies, and our lands.✦ 19 Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land⌘? Buy us and our land for bread, and we and our land will be servants to Pharaoh. Give us seed, that we may live, and not die, and that the land won’t be desolate.”✦ 20 So Joseph bought all the land⌘ of Egypt for Pharaoh, for every man⌘ of the Egyptians sold his field, because the famine was severe on them, and the land became Pharaoh’s.✦ 21 As for the people, he moved them to the cities from one end of the border of Egypt even to the other end of it.✦ 22 Only he didn’t buy the land⌘ of the priests, for the priests had a portion from Pharaoh, and ate their portion which Pharaoh gave them. That is why they didn’t sell their land.✦ 23 Then Joseph said to the people, “Behold, I have bought you and your land⌘ today for Pharaoh. Behold, here is seed for you, and you shall sow the land.✦ 24 It will happen at the harvests, that you shall give a fifth to Pharaoh, and four parts will be your own, for seed of the field, for your food, for them of your households, and for food for your little ones.”✦ 25 They said, “You have saved our lives! Let us find favor in the sight of my lord⌘, and we will be Pharaoh’s servants◇.”✦ 26 Joseph made it a statute concerning the land⌘ of Egypt to this day, that Pharaoh should have the fifth. Only the land of the priests alone didn’t become Pharaoh’s.✦ 27 Israel lived in the land⌘ of Egypt, in the land of Goshen; and they got themselves possessions therein, and were fruitful, and multiplied exceedingly.✦ 28 Jacob lived in the land⌘ of Egypt seventeen years. So the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were one hundred forty-seven years.✦⌂ 29 The time came near that Israel must die, and he called his son Joseph, and said to him, “If now I have found favor in your sight, please put your hand under my thigh◇, and deal kindly and truly with me. Please don’t bury me in Egypt,✦ 30 but when I sleep with my fathers, you shall carry me out of Egypt, and bury me in their burying place.” Joseph said, “I will do as you have said.”✦ 31 Israel said, “Swear to me,” and he swore to him. Then Israel bowed himself on the bed’s head◇.

48

✦1 After these things, someone said to Joseph, “Behold, your father is sick.”

He took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.✦ 2 Someone told Jacob, and said, “Behold, your son Joseph comes to you,” and Israel strengthened himself, and sat on the bed. 3 Jacob said to Joseph, “God⌘ Almighty appeared to me at Luz◇ in the land⌘ of Canaan, and blessed me, 4 and said to me, ‘Behold, I will make you fruitful, and multiply you, and I will make of you a company of peoples, and will give this land⌘ to your offspring after you for an everlasting possession.’ 5 Now your two sons, who were born to you in the land⌘ of Egypt before I came to you into Egypt, are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh, even as Reuben and Simeon, will be mine◇.✦ 6 Your offspring, whom you become the father of after them, will be yours. They will be called after the name of their brothers in their inheritance.✦ 7 As for me, when I came from Paddan, Rachel died beside me in the land⌘ of Canaan on the way, when there was still some distance to come to Ephrath, and I buried her there on the way to Ephrath (also called Bethlehem).”✦⌂ 8 Israel saw Joseph’s sons, and said, “Who are these?”✦ 9 Joseph said to his father, “They are my sons, whom God⌘ has given me here.” He said, “Please bring them to me, and I will bless them.”✦ 10 Now the eyes of Israel were dim for age, so that he couldn’t see well. Joseph brought them near to him; and he kissed them, and embraced them.✦ 11 Israel said to Joseph, “I didn’t think I would see your face, and behold, God⌘ has let me see your offspring also.”✦ 12 Joseph brought them out from between his knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth⌘.✦ 13 Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel’s right hand, and brought them near to him.✦ 14 Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it on Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh’s head, guiding his hands knowingly◇, for Manasseh was the firstborn.✦ 15 He blessed Joseph, and said, “The God⌘ before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me◇ all my life long to this day,✦ 16 the angel who has redeemed me◇ from all evil, bless the lads, and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac. Let them grow into a multitude upon the earth⌘.”✦ 17 When Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand on the head of Ephraim, it displeased him. He held up his father’s hand, to remove it from Ephraim’s head to Manasseh’s head.✦ 18 Joseph said to his father, “Not so, my father, for this is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head.”✦ 19 His father refused, and said, “I know, my son, I know. He also will become a people, and he also will be great. However, his younger brother will be greater than he◇, and his offspring will become a multitude of nations.”✦ 20 He blessed them that day, saying, “Israel will bless in you, saying, ‘God⌘ make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh◇’” He set Ephraim before Manasseh.✦ 21 Israel said to Joseph, “Behold, I am dying, but God⌘ will be with you, and bring you again to the land⌘ of your fathers.✦ 22 Moreover I have given to you one portion above your brothers, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow.”

49

✦1 Jacob called to his sons, and said: “Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you that which will happen to you in the days to come◇.✦ 2 Assemble yourselves, and hear, you sons of Jacob. Listen to Israel, your father.✦ 3 “Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my strength, excelling in dignity, and excelling in power.✦ 4 Boiling over like water⌘◇, you shall not excel, because you went up to your father’s bed, then defiled it. He went up to my couch.✦⌂ 5 “Simeon and Levi are brothers. Their swords are weapons of violence.✧✦⌂ 6 My soul⌘, don’t come into their council. My glory, don’t be united to their assembly; for in their anger they killed men. In their self-will they hamstrung cattle.⌘✦ 7 Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel. I will divide them in Jacob◇, and scatter them in Israel.✦ 8 “Judah, your brothers will praise you. Your hand will be on the neck of your enemies. Your father’s sons will bow down before you.✦ 9 Judah is a lion’s cub. From the prey, my son, you have gone up. He stooped down, he crouched as a lion, as a lioness. Who will rouse him up?✦ 10 The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs◇. The obedience of the peoples will be to him.‖✦◇⌂⌂⌂ 11 Binding his foal to the vine, his donkey’s colt to the choice vine, he has washed his garments in wine, his robes in the blood⌘ of grapes.✦ 12 His eyes will be red with wine, his teeth white with milk.✦⌂ 13 “Zebulun will dwell at the haven of the sea. He will be for a haven of ships. His border will be on Sidon.✦⌂ 14✦ 15 “Issachar is a strong donkey, lying down between the saddlebags. He saw a resting place, that it was good⌘, the land⌘, that it was pleasant. He bows his shoulder to the burden, and becomes a servant doing forced labor.✦ 16 “Dan will judge his people, as one of the tribes of Israel.✦ 17 Dan will be a serpent⌘ on the trail, an adder in the path, that bites the horse’s heels, so that his rider falls backward.✦⌂ 18 I have waited for your salvation⌘, Yahweh.⌘✦ 19 “A troop will press on Gad, but he will press on their heel.✦ 20 “Asher’s food will be rich. He will produce royal dainties.✦ 21 “Naphtali is a doe set free, who bears beautiful fawns.✦⌂ 22 “Joseph is a fruitful vine, a fruitful vine by a spring. His branches run over the wall.✦ 23 The archers have severely grieved him, shot at him, and persecuted him:✦ 24 But his bow remained strong. The arms of his hands were made strong, by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob◇, (from there is the shepherd, the stone of Israel),⌘✦ 25 even by the God⌘ of your father, who will help you, by the Almighty, who will bless you, with blessings of heaven⌘ above, blessings of the deep⌘ that lies below, blessings of the breasts, and of the womb.✦ 26 The blessings of your father have prevailed above the blessings of my ancestors, above the boundaries of the ancient hills. They will be on the head of Joseph, on the crown of the head of him who is separated from his brothers.✦ 27 “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf. In the morning he will devour the prey. At evening he will divide the plunder.”✦⌂ 28 All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father spoke to them, and blessed them. He blessed everyone according to his own blessing.✦ 29 He instructed them, and said to them, “I am to be gathered to my people. Bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field◇ of Ephron the Hittite,✦ 30 in the cave that is in the field of Machpelah, which is before Mamre, in the land⌘ of Canaan, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place.✦ 31 There they buried Abraham and Sarah, his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah, his wife, and there I buried Leah:✦ 32 the field and the cave that is therein, which was purchased from the children of Heth.”✦ 33 When Jacob finished charging his sons, he gathered up his feet into the bed◇, breathed his last breath, and was gathered to his people.

50

✦1✦ 2 Joseph fell on his father’s face, wept on him, and kissed him. Joseph commanded his servants, the physicians, to embalm his father◇; and the physicians embalmed Israel.✦⌂ 3 Forty days were used for him, for that is how many days it takes to embalm. The Egyptians wept for Israel for seventy days.✦ 4 When the days of weeping for him were past, Joseph spoke to Pharaoh’s staff, saying, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, please speak in the ears of Pharaoh, saying,✦⌂ 5 ‘My father made me swear, saying, “Behold, I am dying. Bury me in my grave which I have dug for myself in the land⌘ of Canaan.” Now therefore, please let me go up and bury my father, and I will come again.’”✦ 6 Pharaoh said, “Go up, and bury your father, just like he made you swear.”✦ 7 Joseph went up to bury his father; and with him went up all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his house, all the elders of the land⌘ of Egypt◇,✦⌂ 8 all the house of Joseph, his brothers, and his father’s house. Only their little ones, their flocks, and their herds, they left in the land⌘ of Goshen.✦ 9 Both chariots and horsemen went up with him. It was a very great company.✦ 10 They came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan, and there they lamented with a very great and severe lamentation. He mourned for his father seven days.✦⌂⌂ 11 When the inhabitants of the land⌘, the Canaanites, saw the mourning in the floor of Atad, they said, “This is a grievous mourning by the Egyptians.” Therefore its name was called Abel Mizraim, which is beyond the Jordan.✦ 12 His sons did to him just as he commanded them,✦ 13 for his sons carried him into the land⌘ of Canaan, and buried him in the cave of the field of Machpelah, which Abraham bought with the field, as a possession for a burial site, from Ephron the Hittite, near Mamre.✦ 14 Joseph returned into Egypt—he, and his brothers, and all that went up with him to bury his father, after he had buried his father.✦ 15 When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “It may be that Joseph will hate us, and will fully pay us back for all the evil which we did to him.”✦ 16 They sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father commanded before he died, saying,✦ 17 ‘You shall tell Joseph, “Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers◇, and their sin⌘, because they did evil to you.”’ Now, please forgive the disobedience of the servants of the God⌘ of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him.✦ 18 His brothers also went and fell down before his face; and they said, “Behold, we are your servants.”✦ 19 Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God⌘?⌘✦ 20 As for you, you meant evil against me, but God⌘ meant it for good⌘◇, to save many people alive, as is happening today.‖‖✦◇ 21 Now therefore don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.⌘✦ 22 Joseph lived in Egypt, he, and his father’s house. Joseph lived one hundred ten years.✦ 23 Joseph saw Ephraim’s children to the third generation. The children also of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were born on Joseph’s knees.✧✦ 24 Joseph said to his brothers, “I am dying, but God⌘ will surely visit you◇, and bring you up out of this land⌘ to the land which he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.”✦ 25 Joseph took an oath from the children of Israel, saying, “God⌘ will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones◇ from here.”✦ 26 So Joseph died, being one hundred ten years old, and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt◇.✦⌂

◇ Note. Jacob’s ladder. The Hebrew sullam may better translate as "ramp" or "stairway" — likely the same architectural image as the ziggurat of Genesis 11, but here legitimately connecting heaven and earth. Jesus alludes to this verse in John 1:51 ("you will see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man") — placing himself in the role of the ladder.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And God said unto him, Thy name is Jacob: thy name shall not be called any more Jacob, but Israel shall be thy name'. Ephrem notes the divine reconfirmation: the angelic Jabbok name-change is now RATIFIED by God Himself in direct theophany. The pattern of double-confirmation (angelic-then-divine) is preserved in Tewahedo sacramental practice: the deacon's prayer precedes the priest's consecration; the bishop's chrismation ratifies the presbyter's baptism. Authority moves in stages, never bypassed.

◇ Note. Ben-oni / Benjamin. Rachel names her dying-birth child Ben-oni ("son of my sorrow"); Jacob renames him Binyamin ("son of the right hand," or "son of the south"). One of the few moments in scripture where a parental naming is overridden. Jacob’s renaming is theological — he refuses to let a beloved son carry his mother’s death as his lifelong identity. Rachel is buried on the road to Bethlehem (35:19) — her tomb becomes a pilgrimage site referenced in Jer 31:15 and Matt 2:18.

◇ Note. Levirate marriage. The institution that requires a brother to marry his deceased brother’s childless widow to "raise up offspring" for the dead. Codified in Deut 25:5–10. The Tamar / Onan / Judah narrative (Gen 38) is the Bible’s first extended case study; the book of Ruth is the second. Onan’s "spilling on the ground" is what the modern English word onanism derives from — though the text’s concern is the breach of levirate duty, not contraception per se.

◇ Note. Joseph’s self-revelation. The recognition scene that resolves the cycle. Joseph’s words in 45:5–8 articulate one of the Bible’s major theological claims: "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (50:20). The Joseph cycle (chs 37–50) is widely admired as the most novelistic narrative in the Pentateuch — sustained character development, dramatic irony, no overt theological statements until this revelation. The literary technique reaches its peak here.

◇ Note. Shiloh. The crux of Jacob’s blessing of Judah. The Hebrew shiloh has been read variously: as a place name (Shiloh), as "tribute belongs to him" (shai loh), as "until that which is his comes" (she-loh). The Targums read the verse messianically and translate "until the Messiah comes." Christian tradition takes it as a Messianic prophecy fulfilled in Jesus from the line of Judah. The Dead Sea Scrolls (4QPatriarchal Blessings) read it explicitly of the messianic king. The phrase "obedience of the peoples" anticipates the universal-recognition theme of Isa 49 and elsewhere.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it'. Ephrem reads the ladder as a Christ-Mary type: the ladder is Christ (Jn 1:51 — 'angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man'), AND the ladder is Mary (because she bridges earth and heaven, bringing God to earth and lifting earth to God). Tewahedo Marian hymnody preserves the Jacob-ladder typology as one of Mary's most prominent OT types, in the Wǝddase Maryam (Praise of Mary).

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven'. Ephrem reads Bethel ('house of God') as the proto-temple, proto-church, proto-tabot. Tewahedo ecclesiology explicitly carries the gate-of-heaven identification through every Tewahedo church: each parish church is in some sense Bethel — a renewed-Jacob place where heaven opens. The Tewahedo qǝddase opens with this consciousness.

⌘ Hebrew. Mah nora ha-maqom ha-zeh (מַה־נּוֹרָא הַמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה). The root y-r-a denotes the trembling reverence proper to encountering the holy. The verse coined the Jewish liturgical phrase used at synagogue dedications and holiness moments. Maqom, "place," later becomes a rabbinic divine name — "The Place" = God who is the place of all places.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day'. Ephrem reads the mysterious wrestler as the pre-incarnate Word — the same Person who later appears to Joshua as captain of the Lord's host (Josh 5:13-15) and who ultimately becomes incarnate in Mary's womb. Tewahedo Christology preserves the wrestling-with-the-pre-incarnate-Word as the canonical OT Christophany that establishes the principle: theophany in the OT is always the Son, never the Father.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed'. Ephrem reads the new name as won-not-given: unlike Abraham's name change (simple divine declaration), Jacob WRESTLES for his new name. Tewahedo monastic-ascetical tradition uses this verse as the canonical warrant for spiritual struggle: some names (i.e., spiritual identities) are not handed over but must be wrested through prayer-as-combat. The monastic name received at tonsure is in this lineage.

⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ISRAEL the name conferred on Jacob after the great prayer-struggle at Peniel (Genesis 32:28), because “as a prince he had power with God and prevailed.” (See JACOB.) This is the common name given to Jacob’s descendants. The whole people of the twelve tribes are called “Israelites,” the “children of Israel” (Joshua 3:17; 7:25; Judges 8:27; Jeremiah 3:21), and the “house of Israel” (Exodus 16:31; 40:38). This name Israel is sometimes used emphatically for the true Israel (Psalm 73:1:… [Reviewer: condense Easton's entry as needed.]

⌘ Hebrew. Yisra’el (יִשְׂרָאֵל). The patriarchal renaming. Two etymologies: (1) sarah ‘im El — "he strives with God," matching the angel’s explanation; (2) El yisreh — "God strives," or "God prevails." The very name of the people is built around a wrestling match with the divine — a foundational image of Israel’s relation to God: contention rather than easy submission.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children... and he made him a coat of many colours'. Ephrem reads the ketonet-passim (coat of many colours / long-sleeved tunic) as a PRIESTLY garment — the Septuagint's poikilon resonates with priestly vestment language. Jacob's gift to Joseph is implicit priestly-investiture. Tewahedo liturgical vestments preserve the multi-coloured-tunic pattern in the deacon's and priest's robes: the colours are not decorative but PROPHETIC, drawing on Joseph's typology.

⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CHILD T his word has considerable latitude of meaning in Scripture. Thus Joseph is called a child at the time when he was probably about sixteen years of age (Genesis 37:3); and Benjamin is so called when he was above thirty years (44:20). Solomon called himself a little child when he came to the kingdom (1 Kings 3:7). The descendants of a man, however remote, are called his children; as, “the children of Edom,” “the children of Moab,” “the children of Israel.” In the earliest times… [Reviewer: condense Easton's entry as needed.]

◇ Note. Joseph’s coat. The Hebrew k’tonet passim appears only here and in 2 Sam 13:18, where it describes a princess’s garment. "Many colors" (KJV) is from the LXX chitōna poikilon; the Hebrew probably means "long-sleeved" or "ornamented" — a robe of distinction, marking Joseph as Jacob’s appointed heir over his brothers. Its tearing and bloodying (37:31–33) becomes the symbol of fraternal betrayal.

◇ Note. The Hebrew/Greek divergence. MT reads ha-mittah ("the bed"); LXX reads tēs rhabdou = ha-matteh ("the staff") — the same consonants, different vowels. Hebrews 11:21 follows the LXX ("worshipped, leaning on the top of his staff"). One of the classic places where the NT cites the Greek where it differs from the Hebrew, evidence that the LXX was the working scripture of the early church.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive'. Ephrem treats this verse as the providence-formula par excellence — the complete two-tier reading of history. Tewahedo providential-theology cites Gen 50:20 in close conjunction with Rom 8:28 ('all things work together for good to them that love God') as the OT-NT providence-pair. The verse is foundational in Tewahedo consolation literature: every personal harm submits to the larger divine purpose without thereby being justified or made non-harmful.

◇ Note. The theological summit of Genesis. Joseph’s farewell to his brothers compresses the whole cycle into one sentence. "You meant evil… God meant it for good" articulates the Bible’s most distinctive claim about divine providence — that God works through, not around, human agency, including human evil, without endorsing or causing it. Romans 8:28 reactivates the same theology. The Joseph cycle, the most novelistic narrative in the Pentateuch, ends with its most theological line.

⌘ Hebrew. Ya‘aqov (יַעֲקֹב) — "supplanter." Esau’s bitter pun on his brother’s name plays on the Hebrew root ‘qb, which means "heel" but in verb form means "to seize by the heel, to supplant, to deceive." Jacob (Ya‘aqov) was so named because he came out grasping Esau’s heel at birth (25:26); now Esau retroactively reads the name as predictive: "twice he has supplanted (ya‘qveni) me" — taking the birthright in ch 25, the blessing in ch 27. The naming-becomes-destiny pattern is one of Genesis’s recurring literary devices: names predict (Jacob, Esau, Edom, Babel, etc.). Hosea later picks up the same wordplay: "in the womb he supplanted (‘aqav) his brother" (Hos 12:3). The pun is also theological: Jacob’s name will eventually be changed to "Israel" (32:28), explicitly contrasted with the supplanting-name. The change marks the central theological transformation of the Jacob narrative — from supplanter to wrestler-with-God.

◇ Note. Rebekah’s pretext. Rebekah’s complaint about Esau’s Hittite wives gives Isaac a culturally acceptable reason to send Jacob away to Paddan-aram — but the real reason, hidden from Isaac, is that Esau intends to kill Jacob (27:41–45). The chapter is one of Genesis’s most sophisticated portraits of family-political maneuvering: Rebekah orchestrates the deceptive blessing, then orchestrates Jacob’s escape under cover of marriage-arranging, never telling Isaac the violent truth. The episode also registers a recurring patriarchal-narrative concern with endogamous marriage — Abraham’s servant goes to Mesopotamia for Isaac’s wife (ch 24), Jacob will go to Mesopotamia for his own wives (chs 28–29), and the pattern is theologically loaded: covenant-line marriages stay within the Abrahamic family, while Esau’s exogamous marriages (26:34, "they were a grief of mind to Isaac and to Rebekah") visibly disqualify him from the covenantal succession. Rebekah’s pretext is both excuse and theological diagnosis.

◇ Note. The deceiver deceived. The episode is one of Genesis’s most exquisite narrative ironies: Jacob the deceiver — who used disguised hands and clothing to trick his blind father (ch 27) — is now deceived by Laban using darkness and wedding veil. The Hebrew verb in 29:25 (rimmitani, "you have deceived me") is exactly the verb Isaac used of Jacob in 27:35 (b’mirmah, "with deceit"). The narrator does not comment, but the parallel is structural: Jacob receives in Laban exactly what he gave to Isaac, with the substitution of the older for the younger reversed (Jacob substituted himself the younger for the older Esau; Laban substitutes Leah the older for the younger Rachel). The principle — the deceiver deceived, with the deception precisely calibrated to the original offense — is one of the clearest cases in the OT of measure-for-measure narrative justice. Jacob’s entire Mesopotamian sojourn (chs 29–31) is structured as the working-out of this principle: twenty years of being deceived by Laban purifies Jacob of his deceiver-identity. The verse is the inaugural moment.

⌘ Hebrew. Y’hudah (יְהוּדָה) — "praise." Leah’s fourth son is named from the Hebrew root y-d-h ("to praise, to thank"), with a play on the divine name (Yhwh). The naming-explanation — "this time I will praise Yahweh" — registers a shift in Leah’s pattern: her first three names lament her unloved status (Reuben "see, a son" → reflection on her affliction; Simeon "heard" → Yahweh has heard her affliction; Levi "joined" → maybe now my husband will be joined to me); the fourth name turns from grievance to praise. Through this fourth-named son, the messianic line will run: Judah → David → Christ. The transformation in Leah’s naming-rhetoric prefigures the theological centrality her line will eventually carry. Jacob’s deathbed blessing (Gen 49:8–12) makes Judah the bearer of the royal scepter — and the name itself ("praise") becomes one of the structural keywords of the Davidic-messianic tradition. The verse is one of the OT’s most consequential single naming-moments.

◇ Note. The mandrake episode. Mandrakes (Hebrew duda’im) — yellowish fruits of Mandragora officinarum, the root vaguely man-shaped — were widely understood across the ANE as fertility-aphrodisiacs and aids to conception. The episode is one of the OT’s most strikingly domestic-biological scenes: Reuben finds mandrakes in the field, Rachel (the barren-favored wife) trades a night with Jacob to Leah (the fertile-rejected wife) for them. The transaction reveals the depth of the wife-rivalry that drives the chapter: Rachel will sell her marital privilege for what she hopes will fix her infertility. The episode does not work as Rachel hopes — Leah conceives Issachar from this very night (30:17–18), while Rachel’s eventual conception of Joseph (30:22) is attributed to Yahweh "remembering" her, not to mandrakes. The narrative quietly subverts the magical assumption: divine action, not folk medicine, opens the womb. Song 7:13 mentions mandrakes again in an erotic context, confirming the cultural association.

◇ Note. Jacob’s peeled rods. Jacob’s scheme to acquire the speckled and striped sheep involves peeling stripes into branches and placing them in the watering-troughs while the flocks breed, on the assumption that visual exposure during conception affects offspring patterning. The technique reflects pre-genetic ANE agricultural folk-belief — the same belief underwrites a number of ancient breeding practices. Modern readers tend to ask whether the technique "really worked"; the narrator’s answer is theologically located: the breeding succeeds because Yahweh prospers Jacob (cf. 31:9, "God has taken away your father’s livestock and given them to me"; 31:11–12, the angelic dream confirming divine-orchestrated breeding outcomes). The chapter is doing two things at once: portraying Jacob’s ANE-typical pre-scientific practice and asserting that the success comes from divine intervention rather than from the practice itself. The verse offers one of the OT’s most striking cases of folk-technology framed within providence-theology.

◇ Note. The teraphim theft. Rachel’s theft of her father’s household idols is one of the OT’s most discussed single details. The teraphim (small household figurines, probably ancestral) likely had legal-inheritance significance in Mesopotamian household practice — the bearer of the teraphim could claim primary inheritance rights, attested in Nuzi tablets. Rachel’s theft therefore may have functioned as a final claim on Laban’s household property (cf. 31:14, where Rachel and Leah complain that Laban has treated them as foreigners and withheld their inheritance). The theft’s narrative consequence is significant: when Laban catches up and searches the camp, Rachel hides the teraphim under a camel-saddle and refuses to rise "because the way of women is on me" (31:34–35) — using menstruation-impurity to keep her father from approaching the saddle. The episode is one of Genesis’s most layered: female agency, household-religion, inheritance-claim, and ritual-impurity all combine in a single brief sequence. Most strikingly, it shows household-idol religion within the patriarchal-line family — a messy reality the narrator records without comment.

◇ Note. The Mizpah benediction. Laban’s closing blessing at Mizpah ("the Lord watch between me and you, when we are absent one from another") has had perhaps the longest devotional afterlife of any single Genesis verse, used as a parting blessing in countless Christian liturgies and as the textual root of the modern "Mizpah" jewelry tradition (broken-heart pendants exchanged at separations). The verse’s narrative context complicates its devotional use significantly: Laban’s "blessing" is in fact a wary boundary-treaty, more covenant of mutual deterrence ("if you afflict my daughters, or take other wives… God is witness," 31:50) than warm valedictory wish. The two parties have just spent twenty years deceiving each other; the Mizpah pillar marks the territorial line they will not cross. The verse’s history of devotional use is one of the OT’s clearest examples of a phrase outliving its narrative context entirely — its weight in modern Christian piety has nothing to do with what it actually means in Genesis 31. The chapter is also significant for naming the place "Galeed" (Hebrew "heap of witness") and "Mizpah" ("watchtower"), two of Genesis’s many name-etiologies.

◇ Note. Esau’s embrace. The reunion is one of Genesis’s most emotionally complex scenes: Jacob has spent the previous chapter terrified of Esau’s vengeance, dividing his camp for safety, sending elaborate gifts, wrestling with God all night for the strength to face his brother — and Esau simply runs, embraces, kisses, and weeps. The expected violence does not materialize. The brother who was supposed to kill Jacob (cf. 27:41) instead enacts forgiveness so complete that Jacob says "I have seen your face as one sees the face of God, and you have accepted me" (33:10). The line connects the encounter with Esau directly to Jacob’s previous-night encounter with God at Peniel (32:30, "I have seen God face to face"). The parallel is theological: Jacob meets God in his struggling brother just as he met God at the ford. Esau, in his moment of unexpected mercy, becomes the divine face. The episode is one of the OT’s most extraordinary portraits of forgiveness — not earned, not negotiated, simply offered. Walter Brueggemann reads ch 33 as one of the canon’s most surprising theological moments.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept'. Ephrem reads the reconciliation of the brothers as a foretaste of the eschatological reconciliation promised in Rom 11:25-26 (the fullness of the Gentiles, then all Israel saved). Tewahedo ecumenical theology — preserved in the long Tewahedo refusal to demonize other communions even during Chalcedonian controversies — draws on the Esau-Jacob embrace as canonical model for inter-Christian relations.

⌘ Hebrew. El Elohe Yisrael (אֵל אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל) — "God, the God of Israel." Jacob’s altar at Shechem bears one of Genesis’s most theologically dense names: El (the broader Northwest Semitic divine name, used as title or proper name across Canaanite religion) is named as Elohei Yisra’el ("the God of Israel"). The naming registers Jacob’s identity-shift after Peniel — he is now Israel, and his altar identifies the deity as his God, the God specifically of his line. The construction "El the God of Israel" also works theologically as identification: the high god El of the broader Levantine pantheon is named here as functionally identical with the deity who has shepherded Jacob. Most modern OT scholarship (so Cross, Smith) reads such constructions as evidence of the gradual Israelite absorption of El-traditions into Yahwism — Yahweh and El were not always identified, but the patriarchal narratives increasingly identify them as the same. Jacob’s altar-name preserves an older theological moment, before that identification was fully developed. The verse is one of the OT’s most important pieces of evidence for the historical development of Israelite monotheism.

◇ Note. The rape of Dinah. The chapter opens with one of the OT’s starkest portrayals of sexual violence: Shechem, the prince of the local city, takes Dinah and "humbles her" (Hebrew vay’anneha, the same verb used of sexual violation throughout OT law — Deut 22:24, 29). The narrative complications begin immediately: Shechem then "loved the young woman" (34:3) and proposes marriage. The text refuses easy readings — what begins as violation transitions into proposed alliance, and Dinah herself never speaks. Phyllis Trible’s and Mieke Bal’s feminist readings have made this chapter central to OT scholarship on gendered violence and silence. The brothers’ vengeance — Simeon and Levi’s deceitful slaughter of all the Shechemite men, while convalescent from circumcision — Jacob deplores but does not retract; his deathbed curse on Simeon and Levi (49:5–7) traces directly to this episode. The chapter encodes one of the OT’s most morally unresolved single narratives.

◇ Note. Jacob’s realpolitik. Jacob’s rebuke of Simeon and Levi after their slaughter at Shechem is striking for what it does not say: there is no moral censure of the killing itself, only practical complaint that the violence has made the family politically vulnerable ("I shall be destroyed, I and my house"). The brothers’ retort — "Should he treat our sister as a prostitute?" (34:31) — defends honor; Jacob defends survival. The narrative leaves the moral evaluation to the reader and to Jacob’s deathbed (49:5–7), where Jacob finally pronounces the moral judgment ("cursed be their anger… I will scatter them in Jacob"). The delayed verdict is a Genesis literary signature: moral judgments often arrive chapters or generations after the events, distributed across the canon (Simeon’s eventual absorption into Judah, Lev’s scattering across the tribes). The chapter establishes the principle: actions have consequences that take time to ripen. The Shechem episode’s long aftermath runs through the rest of the patriarchal narrative.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'Now these are the generations of Esau, who is Edom'. Ephrem reads the Edom-genealogy as the FAITHFUL recording of the rejected line — Scripture preserves Esau's descendants not to praise but to remember. Tewahedo historiographical tradition preserves the principle: even the rejected names are recorded, because divine memory excludes no one. The Mäṣḥafä Sǝnksar (Tewahedo Synaxarium) preserves names of heretics and apostates in this same spirit — for memory, not for veneration.

◇ Note. Esau as Edom. The chapter is the OT’s most extended Edomite genealogy, identifying Esau as the eponymous ancestor of Edom — the people who occupied the highlands south and east of the Dead Sea (Mount Seir). The fraternal-rival relationship between Israel and Edom runs through the entire OT: Edomite resistance during the wilderness period (Num 20:14–21), David’s subjugation of Edom (2 Sam 8:13–14), Edom’s opportunistic violence against Judah during the Babylonian destruction (Ps 137:7, Obadiah’s entire prophecy), and the Maccabean-era forced conversion of Idumea (the Greek name for Edom). The chapter’s placement here — extended Edomite genealogy before the resumption of Joseph-cycle narrative in ch 37 — frames the ongoing canonical contrast: Esau’s line becomes a kingdom rapidly (36:31, "before any king reigned over the children of Israel"); Jacob’s line becomes Israel slowly. The chapter’s detail registers the OT’s recurring fascination with the elder-brother lineage: even when not chosen, Esau’s descendants matter, and Genesis preserves their record in detail.

◇ Note. The Edomite kings list. The chapter lists eight kings of Edom by name with succession pattern, then tribal chieftains. The introductory formula — "before any king reigned over the children of Israel" — is one of the OT’s strongest internal indicators of post-monarchic dating: the editor is writing from a vantage point at which Israel does have kings, looking back to a period when Edom did but Israel did not. Most modern critical scholarship treats the formula as one of the clearest signals that Genesis as a finished work cannot be earlier than Saul’s reign (the first Israelite king, ca. 1020 BCE), with most placing the final compilation considerably later. The chapter is therefore unusually transparent about its own historical perspective. Theologically, the verse registers a striking observation: Esau’s line organized into stable monarchy long before Jacob’s line did. The OT does not interpret this as Esau’s superiority; rather, monarchy itself is theologically ambivalent in the OT (1 Sam 8). Edom’s precocity in monarchy is, on the deuteronomistic reading, not an advantage but an early symptom of a different political-religious trajectory.

◇ Note. Joseph’s refusal. The verse contains the OT’s most concentrated single articulation of moral integrity under sexual temptation. Joseph’s reasoning is theologically precise: the wrong is not primarily against Potiphar (though Potiphar’s trust would be betrayed), nor against Potiphar’s wife (though she would be implicated in transgression), but "against God." The episode is one of the OT’s clearest demonstrations that ethics is grounded vertically in covenantal relationship before it is grounded horizontally in social obligation. The detail is also narratively significant: Joseph refuses what would be (in ANE court culture) ordinary opportunistic advancement — a powerful patron’s wife’s favor — and pays for the refusal with imprisonment. The chapter’s subsequent vindication theology (39:21–23, Yahweh’s favor in prison) makes the moral framework clear: integrity costs short-term, but Yahweh’s providence eventually reverses the apparent loss. Joseph’s rise to the second highest position in Egypt comes through, not despite, this initial integrity. The episode is one of the OT’s clearest Wisdom-narrative anticipations of the Proverbs theme of righteous suffering vindicated.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'There is none greater in this house than I; neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?' Ephrem reads Joseph's reasoning as a perfect model of conscience: he refuses on FAITHFULNESS-to-Potiphar AND on faithfulness-to-God. Tewahedo monastic-ethical tradition cites Joseph as the canonical chastity-model: the rejection is reasoned, not just instinctive.

◇ Note. "Yahweh was with him." The phrase ("the LORD was with Joseph") forms one of the chapter’s structural refrains, occurring at 39:2, 21, and 23 — bracketing both the rise in Potiphar’s house and the descent into prison. The narrative point is theologically subtle: the same divine presence that made Joseph prosper in Potiphar’s house follows him into the prison and produces favor with the warden there too. Yahweh’s being-with does not exempt Joseph from suffering or false accusation; it operates within those circumstances rather than removing them. The chapter is one of the OT’s sharpest articulations of providence-through-suffering — a theological pattern that becomes structural in OT and NT both (Job, the Servant Songs of Isa 40–55, Christ’s passion). The Joseph cycle as a whole works out this principle at length: every apparent setback (sold into slavery, falsely imprisoned, forgotten by the cupbearer) becomes the necessary precondition for the next stage of his eventual rise to Pharaoh’s second-in-command. The verse is the chapter’s theological center.

◇ Note. The dream-interpretation principle. Joseph’s answer to the cupbearer and baker — "do not interpretations belong to God?" — establishes the entire theological framework for the dream sequences in chs 40–41. The principle is precise: dream-content comes from God; correct interpretation also comes from God; the human interpreter is merely the divinely enabled mediator. The principle distinguishes Joseph’s practice from professional Egyptian dream-interpreters (Egyptian dream books were extensive, with elaborate symbolic dictionaries; cf. the Chester Beatty dream-papyri). Joseph rejects the technical-professional model in favor of a charismatic-revelational one: each interpretation requires fresh divine illumination. The same principle structures the Daniel narratives (Dan 2:27–28, "no wise men… can show the king the mystery… but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets") and informs the broader OT theology of prophecy as distinct from divination. The verse is one of the OT’s clearest single-line articulations of the prophet-as-vehicle theology that runs through the entire prophetic tradition.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you'. Ephrem treats Joseph's reply to the cupbearer and baker as foundational for the doctrine of divine charism: interpretation of dreams is not a human skill but a divine gift, channelled through specific persons. Tewahedo prophetic-discernment tradition (the monastic discernment-of-spirits charism) traces theologically to this verse: the discerner DOES the interpreting but the interpretation BELONGS to God.

◇ Note. Joseph’s plea. The chapter ends with a small but devastating detail: Joseph’s appeal to the cupbearer to remember him is not honored. "Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him" (40:23). The result is two more years of prison (41:1) before Joseph is finally summoned to interpret Pharaoh’s dream. The forgotten promise is theologically calibrated: had the cupbearer remembered immediately, Joseph would have been freed before Pharaoh’s dream — and the larger providential pattern (Joseph as Pharaoh’s second-in-command, Egypt prepared for famine, the family of Jacob saved) could not have unfolded. The narrative principle: human forgetfulness becomes the medium of divine timing. The chapter is one of the most sophisticated single deferrals in OT narrative — the theological point of two unnecessary prison years is precisely that they are necessary for the providential timeline. The Joseph cycle as a whole works out this pattern of redemptive delay across multiple chapters.

◇ Note. The brothers’ awakening. Twenty years after selling Joseph into Egyptian slavery, the brothers — confronted by the apparently arbitrary cruelty of "the Egyptian governor" (Joseph in disguise) — recognize their predicament as moral consequence. The Hebrew is striking: "we are guilty (asham) concerning our brother" — the technical legal-ritual word for incurred guilt requiring expiation. The episode is one of the OT’s clearest portraits of long-delayed conscience: the moral reality of an act buried for two decades suddenly emerges in the apparent injustice of a present situation. Joseph, hearing this through an interpreter, has to leave the room to weep (42:24) — the first of his weepings before the brothers in the cycle. The chapter is one of the OT’s sharpest psychological-theological observations: guilt that has been suppressed eventually surfaces, and the surfacing is sometimes triggered by suffering that resembles the suffering originally inflicted. Augustine’s reading of conscience in the Confessions draws explicitly on Joseph-cycle patterns of buried-then-emerging memory.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And he turned himself about from them, and wept; and returned to them again'. Ephrem treats Joseph's hidden weeping as the model of concealed-compassion: Joseph maintains the testing-disguise BUT the compassion is real and ongoing. Tewahedo pastoral-theology preserves this image: shepherds and confessors may need to maintain apparent severity for the penitent's good, but the compassion underneath must always be active.

◇ Note. Jacob’s refusal. Jacob’s flat refusal to send Benjamin to Egypt with the brothers — even when the family is starving — registers the depth of his trauma over Joseph: "his brother is dead, and he only is left." The narrator preserves Jacob’s misperception throughout — Jacob assumes Joseph is dead and treats Rachel’s remaining son Benjamin as the last fragile vestige of his beloved wife’s memory. The chapter is one of the OT’s most painfully ironic: the man Jacob refuses to lose Benjamin to is in fact Joseph, the very son Jacob assumes already lost. The Joseph cycle’s entire dramatic structure depends on this irony — the reader knows what Jacob does not, and the suspense across chs 42–45 is generated by the gap. The verse is also significant for what it implies about the dynamics of Jacob’s remaining family: the older sons (sons of Leah, Bilhah, Zilpah) feel themselves expendable in Jacob’s grief, replaceable, ungrieved-for; only Rachel’s sons — Joseph (presumed dead) and Benjamin — receive Jacob’s full attention. The favoritism that drove the brothers to violence in ch 37 has not been corrected.

◇ Note. Joseph’s second weeping. The Joseph cycle stages four weepings of Joseph before his brothers (42:24, 43:30, 45:2, 46:29, with additional weepings at 50:17 and 50:1 over Jacob’s death). The pattern marks Joseph’s emotional progression toward eventual self-revelation: each weeping is more difficult to conceal, more directly tied to a specific brother (here, Benjamin, whom Joseph has not seen in twenty years). The Hebrew nikhm’ru raḥamav — literally "his bowels grew warm" — uses one of the OT’s strongest somatic-emotional idioms; the inner organs are the seat of compassion in Hebrew anthropology, with the same root behind raḥamim ("compassion, mercies"). The narrative restraint is exquisite: Joseph excuses himself to weep privately, washes his face, controls himself, and returns to the meal as if nothing had happened. The chapter is one of the OT’s most sustained portraits of suppressed emotion controlled across long stretches of public composure. The eventual breaking-point in 45:1–2 is theologically calibrated: when concealment can no longer hold, the truth emerges in tears.

◇ Note. The fivefold portion. Joseph’s deliberate display of favoritism — Benjamin’s portion at the meal is five times larger than the others’ — is one of the chapter’s most theologically loaded details. The narrative suspense is precise: Joseph is testing whether the brothers will resent the favored brother as they once resented him. If they show the same envy that motivated their selling Joseph in ch 37, Joseph will not be able to trust them; if they accept Benjamin’s favor without grievance, the moral repair has happened. The brothers’ silent acceptance ("they drank, and were merry with him") suggests they have changed — the test is implicitly passed. The episode is structural: chs 43–44 are one extended psychological test of the brothers’ moral transformation, with each chapter raising the stakes. The fivefold portion is the test’s opening; the chapter’s closure with the brothers’ unenvious enjoyment of the meal sets up the decisive test of ch 44 (the framing of Benjamin for theft, requiring the brothers to choose whether to abandon him as they once abandoned Joseph).

◇ Note. Judah’s confession. Confronted with the apparent theft (Joseph’s silver cup planted in Benjamin’s sack), Judah does not protest innocence — he confesses guilt. The "iniquity" he confesses is not the theft (which the brothers did not commit) but the original sin of the cycle: selling Joseph into slavery. The Hebrew matza Elohim et avon ("God has found out the iniquity") is one of the OT’s clearest articulations of the moral principle that long-buried sin eventually surfaces under divine providence. The episode marks Judah’s transformation: the brother who proposed selling Joseph (37:26–27) now offers himself as substitute for Benjamin (44:33), shouldering the punishment that should fall on his half-brother. The Hebrew theology of substitutionary atonement — the willing exchange of one person’s suffering for another’s — finds one of its earliest narrative expressions here. Judah’s offer becomes the trigger for Joseph’s self-revelation in ch 45. The chapter is the moral hinge of the entire Joseph cycle.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'Then Judah came near unto him, and said... let thy servant abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord'. Ephrem reads Judah's offering of himself as substitute for Benjamin as the OT type of Christ's substitutionary atonement: Judah (the tribe of the future Messiah) offers himself FOR another, anticipating the action of his great descendant. Tewahedo Christology preserves this typology as a key OT witness to vicarious atonement.

◇ Note. Judah’s substitutionary offer. Judah’s offer to remain in Egypt as Joseph’s slave in Benjamin’s place is one of the OT’s most theologically dense single moments. The structure is precisely substitutionary: Judah names the alternative ("when I come to your servant my father, and the boy is not with us… I shall bear the blame to my father forever," 44:32, 34) and chooses voluntary substitution as the only acceptable resolution. The episode is the moral inverse of ch 37: where the brothers once collectively betrayed Joseph for material gain (twenty pieces of silver), Judah now individually offers himself for Benjamin at total cost. Christian theological tradition has often noted the typological resonance: from the tribe of Judah (cf. 49:8–12), the messianic substitute will come — Christ as offered-substitute is foreshadowed in Judah-as-offered-substitute here. The principle the chapter encodes — voluntary self-substitution as the form moral repair takes — is one of the deepest single theological patterns in the OT, directly echoed by Moses in Exod 32:32 and by the Servant of Isa 53. The verse is the spiritual climax of the cycle.

◇ Note. The descent to Egypt. Yahweh’s final patriarchal-period theophany — to Jacob at Beersheba, on the way down to Egypt — explicitly authorizes the descent that will be the precondition for the entire exodus narrative. The verse closes the patriarchal phase of the Genesis story: Abraham was called up to Canaan (12:1); Jacob is now sent down to Egypt (46:3). The chiastic geographical movement is theologically deliberate: the family must go down before it can come up as Israel. The promise Yahweh attaches ("there I will make of you a great nation") explicitly identifies Egypt as the place where the Abrahamic promise of nationhood will be fulfilled — Israel becomes a nation in Egyptian slavery, not in Canaanite freedom, theologically registering that nationhood is gift in spite of context, not consequence of context. The chapter’s detail of Jacob’s 70-person family (46:8–27) becomes the baseline against which Exodus 1:7 will register multiplication ("the children of Israel were fruitful and increased abundantly"). The descent that the patriarch fears is the actual mechanism of fulfillment.

◇ Note. The reunion at Goshen. Jacob and Joseph’s reunion — twenty-two years after Joseph was sold into slavery — is one of the OT’s most affecting scenes. The narrator’s vocabulary is precise and economical: Joseph "fell on his neck and wept on his neck a long while" (Hebrew od, "still, longer"). The detail of the prolonged weeping, after twenty-two years of bereavement, registers the depth of grief Jacob carried. Jacob’s reply — "now let me die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive" (46:30) — frames his subsequent seventeen years in Egypt as bonus-time after the unexpected restoration. The chapter completes the structural inversion: Jacob, who once saw Joseph’s blood-soaked coat and concluded "a wild beast has devoured him" (37:33), now sees Joseph alive in Pharaoh’s second-chariot. The narrative arc of grief reversed by recognition — death assumed, life discovered — is one of the OT’s most influential narrative patterns, recurring in resurrection-narrative shapes across the canon. The verse is the formal closure of the Joseph cycle’s primary plot.

◇ Note. The double adoption. Jacob’s deathbed adoption of Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons — counted alongside Reuben and Simeon as full tribal patriarchs — has long-running canonical consequences: the resulting twelve-tribe structure of Israel ends up with two tribes from Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh) rather than one (Joseph), with Levi separated from territorial allotment because of priestly status. The bookkeeping math: 12 sons of Jacob, but Levi without territory and Joseph counted twice = the standard 12-tribe territorial list (Reuben, Simeon, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Benjamin, Ephraim, Manasseh). The chapter is also one of the OT’s clearest cases of patriarchal blessing reversing primogeniture: Jacob crosses his hands to put the right-hand blessing on younger Ephraim rather than older Manasseh (48:13–20), repeating the pattern that has run through Genesis (Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Joseph over his older brothers). The verse encodes one of the OT’s structural theological principles: divine election consistently inverts birth-order expectations.

◇ Note. The reversed blessing. Jacob’s explicit affirmation that the younger Ephraim will surpass the older Manasseh — over Joseph’s objection (48:17–18) — is one of the clearest articulations of the elder-younger reversal that runs through Genesis. The historical fulfillment is unambiguous: Ephraim becomes the dominant northern tribe, sometimes even functioning as a synecdoche for the entire northern kingdom (cf. Hosea’s repeated "Ephraim" for the northern kingdom; Isa 7:9, 17). Manasseh, while territorially large (with both western and trans-Jordanian portions), never produces the political-religious significance of Ephraim. The principle the chapter encodes — younger-over-older as the recurring divine pattern — is theologically consistent with the rest of Genesis but stands in continuous tension with the actual ANE legal-cultural premium on primogeniture. The Genesis pattern is theologically deliberate counter-cultural: the deity does not honor the social hierarchy that the surrounding cultures take for granted, but operates by criteria of grace and choice rather than birth-order. Paul will eventually cite the pattern at Rom 9:10–13 to articulate the same principle theologically.

◇ Note. Jacob’s prayer. Jacob’s prayer the night before meeting Esau is one of Genesis’s most emotionally exposed moments. The Hebrew opening — qatonti mi-kol ha-ḥasadim, "I am too small for all the loving-kindnesses" — uses an unusual self-diminishing formula that registers genuine humility: Jacob is acknowledging that the prosperity Yahweh has given him exceeds what he deserves. The prayer’s theological structure is exemplary: invocation of Yahweh as covenant-God of his fathers (32:9), self-abasement (32:10), specific request for protection (32:11), and appeal to divine promise (32:12). The chapter overall is one of the OT’s most carefully constructed sequences: Jacob’s elaborate gifts to Esau (32:13–21), the dispatch of his family across the Jabbok (32:22–23), and finally the all-night wrestling-match with the divine figure (32:24–32). The prayer functions as the chapter’s pivot — Jacob has to come to grips with his own inadequacy before he can face either Esau or the night-stranger. The verse encodes one of the OT’s clearest portraits of authentic prayer.

⌘ Hebrew. Yisra’el (יִשְׂרָאֵל). Jacob’s name-change is reaffirmed here at Bethel after first being given at the Jabbok (32:28). The doubled naming registers narrative weight: this is a permanent identity-shift, not a momentary epithet. The Hebrew etymology offered at 32:28 — "you have striven (sarita) with God and with men, and have prevailed" — produces "Israel" as "one who strives with God" or "God strives." The name will become both the patriarch’s personal name (used interchangeably with "Jacob" through the rest of Genesis) and the entire people’s designation. The principle the renaming encodes — identity through encounter rather than birth — runs through the rest of OT theology: covenant-naming creates community where biology alone could not. The verse is also the chapter’s key theological moment: Bethel ("house of God") becomes the site where the patriarch’s new identity is formally divinely confirmed, not just won wrestling. The chapter establishes Bethel as one of the major patriarchal cultic sites — later abused by Jeroboam’s northern calf-cult (1 Kgs 12:28–33) and condemned by Amos (Amos 4:4, "go to Bethel and transgress").

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And he dreamed yet another dream, and told it his brethren, and said, Behold, I have dreamed a dream more; and, behold, the sun and the moon and the eleven stars made obeisance to me'. Ephrem reads Joseph's astral dream as a Marian prefiguration: Rev 12:1 ('a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars') reuses Joseph's imagery for Mary. Tewahedo Marian iconography preserves the Rev-12 crown imagery, reading Joseph's dream as the OT root.

⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DOTHAN two wells, a famous pasture-ground where Joseph found his brethren watching their flocks. Here, at the suggestion of Judah, they sold him to the Ishmaelite merchants (Genesis 37:17). It is mentioned on monuments in B.C. 1600. It was the residence of Elisha (2 Kings 6:13), and the scene of a remarkable vision of chariots and horses of fire surrounding the mountain on which the city stood. ◇ Note. The sale price. Twenty shekels of silver was the standard price of a young male slave in ANE slave-markets of the Middle Bronze Age — attested in the Code of Hammurabi (§116) and in Mesopotamian and Egyptian commercial records. The narrative detail is precisely period-appropriate; later periods saw slave-prices rise (Lev 27:5 sets the dedication-redemption value of a male 5–20 years old at 20 shekels; Exod 21:32 sets the gore-by-ox compensation for a slave at 30 shekels in a slightly later period). The verse is one of the OT’s small windows on the actual slave-market economics of the patriarchal era, and the price’s historical accuracy is one of several details supporting an early second-millennium-BCE date for the underlying tradition. The Christological echo — Judas’ betrayal price of thirty pieces of silver (Matt 26:15, also citing Zech 11:12–13) — has been read as deliberate intertextual signaling: Judas selling Jesus parallels the brothers selling Joseph, who was their predecessor as righteous-sufferer-vindicated. The verse is the moment the entire Joseph-cycle plot turns on.

◇ Note. Judah’s admission. Tamar’s pregnancy by her father-in-law Judah — through her successful disguise as a prostitute when Judah had failed to give her his third son in levirate marriage — is one of the OT’s most morally complex sub-narratives. Judah’s confession ("she is more righteous than I") acknowledges what the chapter has been building: Tamar’s desperate scheme is theologically vindicated as the proper claim on levirate-obligation that Judah was failing to honor. The episode is structurally important: the chapter is inserted into the Joseph cycle (interrupting the seamless narrative between 37:36 and 39:1) for theological reasons. From this Tamar-Judah union come Perez and Zerah (38:29–30), and from Perez descends the Davidic line (Ruth 4:18–22, 1 Chr 2:5–15). Tamar becomes one of the four named women in the genealogy of Christ (Matt 1:3) — alongside Rahab, Ruth, and "the wife of Uriah." The chapter is the OT’s clearest demonstration that the messianic line runs through morally complex circumstances rather than around them. The verse is the canonical vindication of Tamar’s righteousness.

◇ Note. The Egyptian dream-interpreters. Pharaoh’s court magicians and wise men (Hebrew ḥartummim, the same vocabulary used in Exod 7:11 for Pharaoh’s sorcerers in the plague narratives) cannot interpret his dream — making the stage clear for Joseph’s charismatic-revelational alternative (41:16, "It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer"). Egyptian dream-interpretation was a sophisticated professional discipline, with extensive symbolic dictionaries (cf. the Chester Beatty dream-papyri); their failure here is therefore narratively pointed rather than incidental. The same pattern recurs structurally at Dan 2 (the Babylonian wise men cannot interpret Nebuchadnezzar’s dream), Dan 5 (the Babylonian wise men cannot read the writing on the wall) — both echoing this Joseph-cycle pattern: foreign professional divination fails where Israelite charismatic-revelation succeeds. The chapter is the textual prototype for the wisdom-narrative pattern in which Hebrew protagonists exceed foreign court-experts in their own area of professional competence.

◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And Joseph said unto his brethren, I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?' Ephrem reads the self-revelation as the model of merciful self-disclosure: the brothers, expecting wrath, hear MERCY first. Tewahedo theological-anthropology preserves this pattern: divine self-disclosure in Christ runs ahead of and overwhelms human expectation of judgment. The risen Christ's 'Peace be unto you' to the apostles who abandoned Him is the Joseph-pattern fulfilled.

◇ Note. Joseph’s providence theology. The verse — paired with 50:20 ("you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good") — gives the most concentrated articulation of OT providence theology in the entire canon. The brothers’ act remains evil (the verse does not exonerate them); Yahweh’s overruling sovereignty has nonetheless used their evil for redemptive purposes. The two-level theology — human responsibility for moral choices preserved alongside divine sovereignty over outcomes — becomes one of the OT’s structural theological positions, recurring in Isa 10:5–7 (Assyria as Yahweh’s rod for judgment, but accountable for its own arrogance), Acts 2:23 (Christ "delivered up by the determinate counsel of God" but crucified by "wicked hands"), and Rom 8:28 ("all things work together for good"). The chapter is the OT’s clearest single articulation of the theological framework that holds providence and moral responsibility together without collapsing either. Joseph does not rationalize the brothers’ act; he reads it within a larger frame of divine purpose.

◇ Note. Jacob before Pharaoh. Jacob’s self-description to Pharaoh — "the years of my pilgrimage" (Hebrew m’gurai, "sojournings") — uses the same root that defines patriarchal life as a whole: ger, the resident alien who lives in a land not his own. The patriarchs are "sojourners" in Canaan even though Yahweh has promised them the land; the eschatological fulfillment of land-possession remains future. Heb 11:9–13 picks up exactly this language: "By faith he sojourned (parōikēsen) in the land of promise as in a strange country… they confessed that they were strangers and sojourners on the earth." The verse becomes the OT root of one of the NT’s most powerful spiritual metaphors: the people of God as pilgrims, never fully at home in any earthly arrangement. Jacob’s self-description as having had "few and evil" days (47:9) registers a sober realism about his own life — he does not romanticize the wandering, even as the theological frame retains its dignity. The verse is one of the OT’s most poignant patriarchal self-assessments.

'The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be'. Ephrem reads this as the most explicit messianic prophecy in Genesis: Shiloh = the one to whom (Hebrew shelo = 'his') everything belongs / the one who is sent.
